chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job, the credentials and the codes

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The job and the certifications employers ask for
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare three billing and coding certifications and choose one to aim for.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official NHA, AAPC and AHIMA pages, you will compare three billing and coding certifications and write a study and test plan with dates, with the requirements checked on the official page, not guessed.
A medical coder reads the doctor's notes and turns the diagnosis and the services into codes. A medical biller uses those codes to send a claim to the insurance company and follows it until it is paid. In small offices one person often does both.
Employers often ask for a certification. Three common ones: the Certified Billing and Coding Specialist (CBCS) from NHA, the National Healthcareer Association; the Certified Professional Coder (CPC) from AAPC; and the Certified Coding Associate (CCA) from AHIMA, the American Health Information Management Association.
Each has its own rules. For example, NHA's CBCS asks for a high school diploma or GED plus a training program or supervised work experience. Fees, exam rules and requirements change, so read the official page for each one before you pay for anything. This course prepares you; it does not give you a certificate.
Watch out for programs that promise a job or a certificate in a few days. Ask any school which certification exam it prepares you for, and check that exam on the official page.
Step by step:
- Open the official page for the CBCS (nhanow.com), the CPC (aapc.com) and the CCA (ahima.org).
- For each one, write down who gives it, what you need before the exam, and how you take the exam.
- Look at job posts near you and count which certification they ask for most.
- Pick one to aim for, and write a target month for the test.
Words to know:
- Medical coder: a person who turns the doctor's notes into standard codes.
- Medical biller: a person who sends claims to insurance companies and follows them until they are paid.
- Certification: proof from a testing organization that you passed its exam; also called a credential.
- Claim: a bill sent to an insurance company asking it to pay for a visit.
Official sources:
- NHA: Certified Billing and Coding Specialist (CBCS)
- AAPC: Certified Professional Coder (CPC)
- AHIMA: Certified Coding Associate (CCA)
Try it now: Make a three-column table on paper or in a spreadsheet: CBCS, CPC, CCA. For each, write who gives it and what you need before the exam, taken from the official page. Then look at five local job posts and circle the certification you will aim for.
You can now say what billers and coders do, name three certifications and who gives them, and pick one to aim for.

options: The doctor's office you work for
check.why: The Certified Professional Coder (CPC) is AAPC's certification.

check.q: A website says you can be a certified coder in three days for a small fee. What do you do first?
options: Pay quickly before the price goes up
Check the real exam's rules on the official page
Skip training; the website is enough
check.why: Only the organization that gives the certification can tell you its real rules and exam.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: How a bill moves: the billing cycle
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put the steps of the billing cycle in order, from scheduling to payment.
This lesson builds toward: Given the steps of a doctor visit out of order, you will put the steps of the billing cycle in order, from scheduling to payment, with no step missing.
The billing cycle, also called the revenue cycle, is the path from the moment a patient books a visit to the moment the office is fully paid.
The main steps: 1) Schedule the visit and check the insurance. 2) Check the patient in: confirm their name, date of birth and insurance card. 3) The doctor sees the patient and writes notes. 4) The coder turns the notes into codes. 5) The biller makes the claim and checks it. 6) The claim is sent to the insurance company. 7) The insurance company pays, pays part, or denies it, and sends an explanation. 8) The office bills the patient for what they owe, such as a copay, and follows up on anything unpaid.
Mistakes early in the cycle cause problems later. A wrong insurance number at check-in can get a claim denied weeks later. That is why careful check-in matters as much as careful coding.
Step by step:
- Schedule and check the insurance.
- Check the patient in and confirm their details.
- The doctor sees the patient and writes notes.
- Code the visit.
- Build and check the claim.
- Send the claim.
- Read the payment or denial.
- Bill the patient's share and follow up.
Words to know:
- Billing cycle (revenue cycle): all the steps from booking a visit to being fully paid.
- Copay: a set amount the patient pays for a visit.
- Deductible: the amount a patient pays each year before the insurance starts paying for many services.
- Payer: the insurance company or government program that pays the claim.
- Denial: when the payer refuses to pay a claim.
Try it now: Write the eight steps of the billing cycle on eight scraps of paper. Mix them up, then put them back in order without looking. Next to each step, write one mistake that could happen there, for example a misspelled name at check-in.
You can now list the steps of the billing cycle in order and say how an early mistake can cause a denial later.

check.q: Which step comes right after the coder turns the notes into codes?
options: The biller builds and checks the claim
check.why: Coding comes first; then the biller builds the claim from those codes and checks it.

check.q: At check-in, the patient's insurance number is typed wrong. What is the most likely result?
options: The claim may be denied later
check.why: The payer matches the claim to its member records; a wrong number often leads to a denial.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The three code sets
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Match each part of a visit to the right code set.
This lesson builds toward: Given five parts of a made-up visit, you will match each part to the right code set: ICD-10-CM for the diagnosis, CPT for the doctor's service, HCPCS Level II for supplies, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
A claim answers two questions: why did the patient come in, and what did the office do? Different code sets answer each one.
ICD-10-CM codes say WHY: the diagnosis, sign or symptom. They start with a letter, then numbers, and may have a dot, for example I10 for high blood pressure with no known cause (practice example). In the US, the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) keeps ICD-10-CM.
CPT codes say WHAT the doctor or other professional did: an office visit, a lab test, a procedure. They are five digits, for example 36415 for drawing blood from a vein (practice example). The American Medical Association (AMA) owns and updates CPT. CMS calls CPT "HCPCS Level I".
HCPCS Level II codes cover things CPT does not, like supplies, equipment and ambulance rides. They are one letter and four digits. CMS (the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services) keeps them. All code sets are updated every year, so always use the current book or tool.
Words to know:
- Diagnosis: the health problem the doctor finds or treats.
- ICD-10-CM: the code set for diagnoses in the US.
- CPT: the AMA's five-digit code set for services and procedures; also called HCPCS Level I.
- HCPCS Level II: CMS's code set for supplies, equipment and other items CPT does not cover; one letter and four digits.
- CMS: the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the federal agency that runs Medicare and works with states on Medicaid.
Official sources:
- CDC NCHS: ICD-10-CM
- CMS: HCPCS (Level I is CPT, Level II is kept by CMS)
Try it now: Practice only. For this made-up visit, write the code set for each part: (1) sore throat, (2) office visit with the doctor, (3) rapid strep test, (4) high blood pressure, (5) a pair of crutches the patient takes home. Answers: 1 and 4 are ICD-10-CM, 2 and 3 are CPT, 5 is HCPCS Level II.
You can now say which code set answers why the patient came in and which answers what was done, and match parts of a visit to ICD-10-CM, CPT or HCPCS Level II.

check.q: Which code set do you use for the patient's diagnosis?
check.why: ICD-10-CM codes say why the patient came in: the diagnosis, sign or symptom.

check.q: A patient goes home with a walker. Which code set usually covers the walker?
check.why: Equipment and supplies that CPT does not cover use HCPCS Level II codes.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Looking up a code the right way
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Look up a diagnosis code in the index and confirm it in the code list.
This lesson builds toward: Given a diagnosis from a made-up visit note, you will look up a diagnosis code by finding the term in the index and then confirming it in the code list, every time, never coding from the index alone.
ICD-10-CM has two main parts. The alphabetic index lists conditions by name, like a book index. The tabular list shows every code in order, with notes about when to use it and when not to.
The rule coders follow: find the main word in the index first, then always confirm the code in the tabular list. Never code from the index alone, because the tabular list may say to add a character or use a different code.
Look up the condition, not the body part. For "acute sore throat", the main word is pharyngitis (the medical word for a sore, swollen throat). Then read the notes in the tabular list before you pick the code. CPT has its own index and code list too, and works the same way.
Free practice: the CDC's ICD-10-CM Browser Tool lets you search the code set online. In a real job, you use the current code book or the tool your employer pays for, and the doctor's notes, never a guess.
Step by step:
- Read the doctor's note and find the diagnosis.
- Find the main word for the condition in the alphabetic index.
- Write down the code the index points to.
- Go to that code in the tabular list.
- Read the notes: "includes", "excludes", and whether more characters are needed.
- Pick the code that matches the note exactly.
Words to know:
- Alphabetic index: the part of the code book that lists conditions by name, A to Z.
- Tabular list: the part of the code book that lists every code in order, with rules for using it.
- Main term: the word for the condition you look up first, not the body part.
- Specificity: how exact a code is; coders use the most exact code the doctor's notes support.
Official sources:
- CDC NCHS: ICD-10-CM and the ICD-10-CM Browser Tool
Try it now: Practice only. Open the CDC's ICD-10-CM Browser Tool from the source link. Look up these made-up diagnoses: "acute pharyngitis", "essential hypertension" and "type 2 diabetes without complications". For each, write the main word you searched, the code you found and one note you read before choosing it.
You can now look up a diagnosis code in two steps, index then tabular list, and say why you never stop at the index.

check.q: You found a code in the alphabetic index. What do you do next?
options: Put it on the claim right away
Confirm it in the tabular list and read its notes
Ask the patient if it looks right
check.why: The tabular list has the rules and may need extra characters; never code from the index alone.

check.q: The note says "acute bronchitis". What is the main word to look up?
check.why: You look up the condition (bronchitis), then find "acute" under it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Filling in a claim and fixing a denial
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Fill in the main boxes of a practice 1500 claim and find why a claim was denied.
This lesson builds toward: Given a made-up visit and a blank practice claim form, you will fill in the main claim boxes and find the reason a practice claim was denied, with the patient, insurance, codes and charges matching the visit.
Doctors' offices bill on the 1500 claim form, kept by the National Uniform Claim Committee (NUCC). The paper version in use is the 02/12 form. Most claims are sent electronically today, but the electronic claim has the same information, so learning the paper form teaches you the data.
Main boxes to know (practice): Box 1a, the insured's ID number from the insurance card. Box 2, the patient's name. Box 21, the diagnosis codes, labeled A, B, C and so on. Box 24, the service lines: date of service (24A), the CPT or HCPCS code (24D), the diagnosis pointer that links the service to a diagnosis letter in Box 21 (24E) and the charge (24F). Box 33, the billing provider.
Before a claim goes out, check it: right patient and ID, every service has a diagnosis pointer, codes are current, dates and charges match the visit. Catching mistakes now is cheaper than fixing a denial later.
When a claim is denied, the payer sends a remittance (an explanation of the payment) with a reason. Common reasons: wrong ID or name, missing or invalid code, service not covered, missing prior authorization, a duplicate claim, or sent too late. Find the reason, fix it, and resend or appeal by the payer's rules.
Step by step:
- Copy the insured's ID (1a) and the patient's name (2) exactly from the made-up card.
- Write the diagnosis codes in Box 21 as A, B, C.
- On each service line in Box 24, write the date, the CPT or HCPCS code, the diagnosis pointer and the charge.
- Fill in the billing provider (33).
- Check the claim with your pre-send checklist.
- If it comes back denied, read the reason, fix the cause and resend by the payer's rules.
Words to know:
- 1500 claim form: the standard paper claim form for doctors' offices, kept by the NUCC.
- Diagnosis pointer: the letter on a service line (A, B, C) that links it to a diagnosis in Box 21.
- Remittance (EOB or ERA): the payer's explanation of what it paid or denied, and why.
- Prior authorization: approval from the payer before some services are done.
- Clean claim: a claim with no errors, so it can be paid the first time.
Official sources:
- NUCC: 1500 Claim Form
Try it now: Practice only. Made-up patient: Sam Rivera, insured ID ABC123456. Visit on a date you choose: office visit (99213) for a sore throat (J02.9) with a rapid strep test (87880), charges $100 and $25 (made-up). On paper or in a spreadsheet, fill in Boxes 1a, 2, 21, 24 (two lines) and 33 ("Practice Clinic"). Then the claim comes back: "invalid member ID". Write what you would check and fix.
You can now fill in the main boxes of a practice claim, check it before it goes out, and find and fix the reason for a denial.

check.q: Where do the diagnosis codes go on the 1500 form?
check.why: Box 21 holds the diagnosis codes, lettered A, B, C and so on.

check.q: A claim is denied with "service requires prior authorization". What was missing?
options: The payer's approval before the service
A second copy of the claim
The doctor's signature on the paper chart
check.why: Prior authorization is the payer's approval before some services; without it the claim is denied.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Protecting patient privacy, and your practice claim
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Share patient information only with people who need it, and only what they need.
This lesson builds toward: In practice situations at work, you will share patient information only with people who need it, and only the minimum they need, in every situation, following HIPAA.
Billers and coders see private health information every day: names, birth dates, diagnoses, insurance numbers. HIPAA is the federal law that protects it. Its Privacy Rule covers health plans, most doctors' offices and hospitals, and the companies that work for them, such as billing companies.
Protected health information (PHI) is any health information that can identify a person. The "minimum necessary" rule means you use and share only what is needed for the job. A payer may need the diagnosis code on the claim; a coworker in the break room does not need to hear it.
Everyday habits: lock your screen when you step away, never talk about patients in public, check the identity of anyone who calls, send claims only through approved systems, and never email or text PHI from a personal account. If you see a privacy mistake, tell your supervisor or privacy officer right away.
Now put it all together in your final task: a complete practice claim and your certification plan.
Step by step:
- Before sharing, ask: does this person have a work reason to know?
- Share only the minimum they need.
- Confirm who is calling before you give out anything.
- Lock your screen and use only approved systems.
- Report privacy mistakes to your supervisor or privacy officer.
Words to know:
- HIPAA: the federal law that protects the privacy and security of health information.
- PHI: protected health information: health information that can identify a person.
- Minimum necessary: the HIPAA idea of using or sharing only the information needed for the task.
- Privacy officer: the person at work in charge of privacy rules and reports.
Official sources:
- HHS: HIPAA for professionals (Privacy Rule)
Try it now: Final task, practice only. Made-up visit: Ana Lee, insured ID XYZ987654, sees the doctor (99213) for high blood pressure (I10) and has blood drawn from a vein (36415); made-up charges $100 and $15. Fill in a practice 1500 claim (Boxes 1a, 2, 21, 24, 33), check it with a pre-send checklist you write yourself, and add a one-page plan: your certification, where you will train, and a target test date. Use no real patient information.
You can now protect patient information with the minimum necessary rule and turn a made-up visit into a complete, checked practice claim.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Certification plan No certification named, or requirements guessed instead of checked. Names one certification and who gives it, with requirements and a target test date taken from the official page. Also lists a training program, weekly study dates and what local job posts ask for. Right code sets A diagnosis is coded with CPT, or a service with ICD-10-CM. The diagnosis uses ICD-10-CM and each service uses CPT. Can explain why each code belongs to its code set. Codes looked up the right way Codes copied without checking, or taken from the index alone. Each diagnosis was found in the index and confirmed in the tabular list (or the CDC tool). Notes the main word searched and one rule read for each code. Claim boxes filled in Boxes are missing, or the ID, codes or charges do not match the visit. Boxes 1a, 2, 21, 24 and 33 are filled in and match the visit; every service line has a pointer. Includes a written pre-send checklist that catches at least one planted mistake. Billing cycle and follow-up Cannot say what happens after the claim is sent. Says the steps from sending to payment, and what to do if it is denied. Names two denial reasons and the fix for each. Privacy kept Uses real patient information, or shares PHI with someone who does not need it. Uses only made-up information and keeps the claim private. Lists three daily habits that protect PHI at work. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A caller says she is a patient's sister and asks for his diagnosis. What do you do?
options: Read her the diagnosis to be helpful
Tell her the diagnosis code only
Follow your office's rules to confirm who may get information; do not share it
check.why: HIPAA limits who may get PHI; you follow your office's rules and share nothing until you confirm.

options: Share only the information needed for the task
Code only one diagnosis per claim
check.why: Under HIPAA you use and share only the information needed for the job.
